title: Listing Files with ls 📋
description: Unlock the power of `ls` with `-l`, `-a`, `-h`, `-R` and more options.

slides.title: Meet ls – Your Eyes in the Terminal 👀
slides.content:
## `ls` – List Directory Contents

`ls` shows the files and folders in a directory. Without arguments, it shows the current directory.

Basic usage:
- `ls` – simple listing
- `ls /path` – list a specific directory

quizData.question: What does `ls` without any arguments do?
quizData.explanation: By default, `ls` lists the contents of the working directory.

slides.title: Supercharged Options ⚡
slides.content:
## Add Flags to ls

Flags (options) modify behaviour. They are preceded by a dash `-`.

- `ls -l` – long format (permissions, size, date)
- `ls -a` – all files, including hidden ones (starting with `.`)
- `ls -h` – human‑readable sizes (e.g. 1K, 234M)
- `ls -R` – recursive, list subdirectories too
- `ls -t` – sort by modification time, newest first
- `ls -r` – reverse order

You can combine flags: `ls -lha` shows long format, all files, human sizes.

quizData.question: Which flag would you use to show hidden files?
quizData.explanation: `-a` stands for 'all' and includes files whose names start with a dot.

slides.title: Understanding ls -l Output 🔍
slides.content:
## Decoding the Columns

A line like `-rw-r--r-- 1 alice staff 2048 May 22 10:00 file.txt` gives:

- File type and permissions: `-rw-r--r--`
- Number of links: `1`
- Owner: `alice`
- Group: `staff`
- Size (bytes): `2048`
- Modification date and name.

We'll dive deeper into permissions later.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## ls with Wildcards
`ls *.txt` lists only text files. Wildcards are coming in Lesson 5!
